newsitem.title: SPAIN: Kasparov urges use of laptops in chess matches.
newsitem.headline: Kasparov urges use of laptops in chess matches.

text.p: Six weeks after being beaten by an IBM supercomputer, world chess champion Garry Kasparov proposed on Friday that top players be allowed to use laptop computers to plot strategy during their matches.

"Today people are not only looking for excitement but also for very high quality play. If a professional grandmaster is assisted by a small laptop computer it dramatically increases the quality of their analysis and game," Kasparov said at a news conference.
The 34-year-old Russian player said just as mathematicians rely on calculators, laptops should become an acceptable tool in the game.

"It doesn't help a weak player or even an average player but for the good player it opens new horizons and it could let us play phenomenal games," said Kasparov, who some experts consider the best player in history.
The triumph of IBM's Deep Blue computer over Kasparov in May made chess history -- it was the first time a program defeated a reigning world champion in a classical chess match.
But the humbled grandmaster insisted that the match had been essentially unfair because he had no access to the computer's pre-match games or any of the IBM printouts during the contest.

"I hate losing. I was shocked. I underestimated the machine, but I was angry because I don't think the match was played under fair conditions... now I want a return match but under different conditions," he said.
But IBM has not yet agreed to a rematch.
"The ultimate challenge is to prove that human beings are superior to machines. I think I'm still superior to the machine," he said.

Kasparov also complained that the machine had the support of a team of operators. "I have to sit alone, I cannot talk to my coach but the machine is talking regularly every second to a team of operators," he said.
But despite all its faults, Kasparov still trumpeted the computer as the key to the future of chess and said it would revolutionise the game in the next few years.
"I have strong feelings that in a couple of years every player will be assisted by a small laptop computer," he said.

As regards his own future, Kasparov said he had no plans to retire from the game. "I believe I am the best player. If I go, chess will lose a lot and I don't want chess to lose popularity when it has such a great potential," he said.
